Title: Oncology Initial Evaluation Summary
---
PATIENT: Patient
ID: p01
DOB: [REDACTED]

ATTENDING: Dr. Smith, MD (Medical Oncology)

COMPREHENSIVE ONCOLOGY HISTORY:

This is a 60-year-old male with a significant personal and family history of cancer, consistent with a hereditary cancer syndrome.

1.  **Rectal Cancer (C20.9):** Diagnosed in 1987. He was treated at an outside facility with neoadjuvant chemoradiation (5-FU/Mitomycin and 3000 cGy pelvic radiation) followed by an abdominoperineal resection (APR) resulting in a permanent end colostomy. He is considered cured but with significant long-term effects from pelvic radiation.

2.  **Appendiceal Cancer (C18.1):** Diagnosed in 2005 after presenting with symptoms leading to a laparoscopic appendectomy. Pathology revealed a moderately differentiated mucinous adenocarcinoma, pT3. He declined a recommended right hemicolectomy and was treated with adjuvant capecitabine in 2006. He is currently considered to have no evidence of disease (NED) from this primary.

3.  **Prostate Cancer (C61.9):** Recently diagnosed in July 2015 via transperineal biopsy, prompted by a rising PSA (14.7 ng/mL). Pathology showed prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason Grade Group 3 (3+4), involving 1 of 6 cores (45% of core).

4.  **Hereditary Cancer Syndrome:** His history of three separate primary cancers (rectal, appendiceal, prostate) is highly suspicious for Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC). His family history is also significant for a father who died of colon cancer and a sister who died of metastatic cancer. Formal genetics consultation and testing will be strongly recommended.

CURRENT PRESENTATION:
The patient is referred to JSL Medical Center for management of his newly diagnosed, unfavorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer. The key challenge in his management is his prior pelvic radiation, which significantly constrains treatment options.

ASSESSMENT & PLAN:
1.  **Prostate Cancer:** The patient is not a candidate for brachytherapy due to his absent rectum and prior pelvic radiation. Treatment options discussed are radical prostatectomy (RP) vs. external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). Given his surgical history and prior radiation, both options carry increased risk of morbidity. He is leaning towards radiation-based treatment.
2.  **Genetic Counseling:** Urgent referral to the Cancer Genetics clinic to discuss testing for Lynch Syndrome. This has significant implications for his future cancer risk (e.g., bladder, urothelial, gastric) and for his family members.
3.  **Staging:** Proceed with staging workup for the prostate cancer, including a bone scan and a pelvic MRI to better define the local extent of the disease.
4.  **Multidisciplinary Review:** His case will be presented at the next Genitourinary (GU) Oncology Tumor Board to discuss the complexities of his treatment.

This patient represents a complex clinical case requiring careful multidisciplinary management to navigate his multiple cancer diagnoses and treatment-related constraints.

===== Document 002 =====
Patient Id: p01

Title: MRI PROSTATE W/WO CONTRAST
---
EXAMINATION: MRI PROSTATE W/WO CONTRAST
CLINICAL STATEMENT: Prostate cancer, PSA 15.7 ng/mL. Biopsy in July 2015 showed Gleason 3+4=7. History of Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC), status post APR for rectal cancer in 1987. Staging evaluation.

TECHNIQUE: Multiplanar, multisequence images of the prostate and pelvis were obtained at 3T without and with intravenous administration of gadolinium-based contrast.

COMPARISON: MRI from outside hospital dated May 20, 2015.

FINDINGS:
PROSTATE GLAND: The prostate gland is small, with an estimated volume of 8 cc. Anatomy is distorted due to post-surgical changes from the prior abdominoperineal resection. Extensive metallic artifact from surgical clips limits evaluation, particularly of the gland's posterior aspects and seminal vesicles.

PROSTATE LESIONS:
Compared to the prior study, there are more conspicuous, ill-defined areas of T2 hypointensity with restricted diffusion and early focal enhancement, suspicious for tumor. These are located in:
1. The right base, involving the posterior peripheral and transition zones.
2. The left posterior peripheral zone at the apex.

EXTRACAPSULAR EXTENSION (ECE): Evaluation is severely limited by artifact and distorted anatomy. There is broad abutment of the tumor with the capsule in the right base and left apex posteriorly. No definitive ECE is identified.

SEMINAL VESICLES (SV): The seminal vesicles are not clearly visualized due to post-surgical changes and artifact. SV invasion cannot be excluded.

LYMPH NODES: No pelvic lymphadenopathy is identified.

BONES: A tiny sclerotic lesion is noted in the proximal right femoral diaphysis, likely benign (enostosis). No acute or suspicious osseous lesion to suggest metastasis.

OTHER: Status post-APR with end colostomy noted.

IMPRESSION:
1. Findings suspicious for multifocal prostate cancer, with dominant lesions in the right base and left apex, showing interval increase in conspicuity since the prior MRI from May 2015.
2. Assessment for extracapsular extension and seminal vesicle invasion is severely limited by post-surgical artifact and anatomical distortion. No gross ECE is seen.
3. No evidence of pelvic lymphadenopathy or osseous metastases.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Davis, MD
JSL Medical Center, Department of Radiology

===== Document 004 =====
Patient Id: p01
Doc Id: 004
Filename: p01/jsl_p01_004_clinical_doc.txt
Doc Type: clinical
Date: 2015-10-15
Title: Radiation Oncology Consultation Note
---
PATIENT: Patient
ID: p01

REASON FOR CONSULTATION: Management of unfavorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient is a 60-year-old male with a complex oncologic history, most notably rectal cancer in 1987 treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiation (30 Gy) and APR, and now a new diagnosis of prostate cancer (Gleason 3+4=7, PSA 15.7 ng/mL). He has known Lynch Syndrome. Staging workup (MRI, bone scan) is negative for metastatic disease, though local staging is limited by artifact. He is reluctant to undergo surgery.

ASSESSMENT:
The patient has unfavorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer. His prior pelvic radiation presents a significant challenge. The rectum is absent, precluding brachytherapy. The main options are radical prostatectomy or external beam radiation therapy (EBRT).

DISCUSSION:
We discussed treatment options at length.
1.  **Surgery (RP):** This remains a valid option, but the risks of urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction are high, and the procedure is technically challenging given his prior APR and pelvic scarring.
2.  **EBRT:** This is a feasible alternative. Given his unfavorable-risk features, treatment would be combined with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) for 6 months. We discussed the increased risk of late GU and GI toxicity due to re-irradiation of the pelvis, even with modern techniques. The prior 30 Gy is a significant dose, and further radiation must be planned meticulously to minimize overlap and spare organs at risk, particularly the bladder. There is also a theoretical increased risk of a second malignancy (e.g., bladder cancer) in a patient with Lynch Syndrome receiving pelvic radiation, although the absolute risk is low.

PLAN:
After extensive discussion, the patient expresses his preference to proceed with EBRT and ADT. He understands the risks, including the potential for significant long-term urinary toxicity.
1.  Initiate ADT (e.g., Leuprolide) for 6 months.
2.  Proceed with CT simulation for radiation planning. We will plan for a dose of 75.6 Gy in 42 fractions to the prostate.
3.  Place fiducial markers in the prostate for image guidance during treatment.
4.  Continue multidisciplinary management with Urology and Medical Oncology.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Brown, MD
JSL Medical Center, Department of Radiation Oncology

Title: CT-Guided Fiducial Marker Placement
---
PRE-PROCEDURE DIAGNOSIS: Prostate Cancer (C61.9)

POST-PROCEDURE DIAGNOSIS: Same

PROCEDURE: CT-guided placement of three periprostatic fiducial markers.

INDICATION: Patient undergoing external beam radiation therapy for prostate cancer. Markers are for image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT).

OPERATOR: Dr. Davis, MD (Interventional Radiology)

PROCEDURE DETAILS:
The patient was placed in the prone position on the CT scanner table. After sterile prep and drape, local anesthesia was administered.
Under CT guidance, three solid gold fiducial markers were placed via a transgluteal approach using 18-gauge needles.
The markers were positioned as follows:
- One marker at the prostatic apex.
- One marker at the right prostatic base.
- One marker at the left prostatic base.

Post-procedure imaging confirmed satisfactory placement of all three markers in the periprostatic tissue.

COMPLICATIONS: None. The patient tolerated the procedure well.

IMPRESSION:
Successful CT-guided placement of three periprostatic fiducial markers in preparation for EBRT.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Davis, MD
JSL Medical Center, Department of Interventional Radiology

Title: Urology Follow-Up Note
---
PATIENT: Patient
ID: p01

SUBJECTIVE:
Patient is a 61-year-old male seen for his first post-treatment follow-up. He completed a course of EBRT (75.6 Gy in 42 fractions) for prostate cancer on April 15, 2016. This was combined with 6 months of ADT (last Lupron injection January 28, 2016).
His oncologic history is notable for Lynch syndrome, rectal cancer s/p APR, and appendiceal cancer.
He reports doing reasonably well. He has ongoing fatigue which he attributes to the ADT, but notes it is slowly improving.
Urinary: IPSS is 9/2 (previously 5/3 pre-treatment), mainly frequency which he associates with caffeine. No hematuria or incontinence.
Sexual: IIEF is 5 (previously 6).
Bowel: Ostomy output is normal.

OBJECTIVE:
Vitals: Stable.
Labs:
- PSA (07/28/2016): <0.05 ng/mL (Nadir)
- Testosterone (07/28/2016): 58 ng/dL (still castrate)

ASSESSMENT:
1.  **Prostate Cancer (C61.9):** Status post definitive EBRT and ADT. Excellent response with PSA nadir <0.05 ng/mL. Currently NED.
2.  **Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC):** Stable. Requires ongoing multi-system surveillance.
3.  **Treatment-related side effects:** Mild urinary frequency (cystitis) and fatigue/sexual dysfunction secondary to ADT.

PLAN:
1.  Continue to monitor PSA and testosterone levels. Next check in 6 months.
2.  Recommend continued surveillance for other Lynch-associated cancers, including annual colonoscopy (of stoma/remaining colon) and continued urologic surveillance.
3.  Manage side effects symptomatically. Advised to reduce caffeine intake.
4.  Return to clinic in 9-12 months, or sooner if any issues arise.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Johnson, MD
JSL Medical Center, Department of Urology

Title: Radiation Oncology Follow-Up
---
PATIENT: Patient
ID: p01

SUBJECTIVE:
Patient is a 64-year-old male, s/p EBRT (75.6 Gy) and ADT for prostate cancer, completed in April 2016. He has a history of Lynch syndrome with prior rectal and appendiceal cancers. He presents for routine follow-up.
He reports feeling well overall. However, he notes an episode of gross hematuria approximately one month ago. This was a single episode, which self-resolved. He was seen at a local clinic and given antibiotics, though no formal diagnosis was made.
An MRI of the abdomen, done for his routine colon cancer surveillance in late 2018, incidentally noted a "0.8 cm lesion along the posterior bladder wall." He has not had specific follow-up for this finding yet.
His PSA has been slowly rising but remains low.

OBJECTIVE:
Labs:
- PSA (02/02/2019): 0.23 ng/mL (Previous: 0.11 in Jan 2018)
- Testosterone (02/02/2019): 374 ng/dL (Recovered)

ASSESSMENT:
1.  **Prostate Cancer (C61.9):** Biochemical recurrence (BCR). His PSA is slowly rising from its nadir of <0.05. The doubling time is long, and the absolute value is still very low. This is consistent with a local recurrence.
2.  **New Bladder Lesion / Hematuria:** The combination of gross hematuria and an enhancing bladder lesion on MRI in a patient with Lynch Syndrome and a history of pelvic radiation is highly concerning for a new primary bladder cancer (urothelial carcinoma). This requires urgent evaluation. The history of pelvic radiation is a known risk factor, as is Lynch Syndrome itself.

PLAN:
1.  **Prostate Cancer:** Continue active surveillance with serial PSA monitoring every 6 months. No intervention is indicated at this time for the slow BCR.
2.  **Bladder Lesion:**
    - Urgent referral back to Urology (Dr. Johnson).
    - Recommend CT Urogram to evaluate the entire urinary tract.
    - Recommend urine cytology.
    - He will almost certainly require a cystoscopy with biopsy/resection of the bladder lesion.
3.  Reinforced the importance of the urologic evaluation given his multiple risk factors for urothelial carcinoma.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Brown, MD
JSL Medical Center, Department of Radiation Oncology

EXAMINATION: CT UROGRAM W/WO CONTRAST
CLINICAL STATEMENT: 64-year-old male with history of Lynch syndrome, prior pelvic radiation, and prostate cancer. Recent gross hematuria and 0.8 cm bladder lesion on prior MRI. Evaluate for urothelial carcinoma.

TECHNIQUE: Multiphase CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis was performed without and with intravenous contrast, including non-contrast, nephrographic, and excretory phases.

COMPARISON: Abdominal MRI from 2018.

FINDINGS:
KIDNEYS/URETERS: No hydronephrosis or hydroureter. No filling defects in the upper tracts. Bilateral simple renal cysts are noted.

BLADDER: There is a new, avidly enhancing soft tissue nodule in the left posterior bladder wall, near the trigone. It measures 1.2 x 1.1 cm in maximal dimensions. This corresponds to the lesion seen on the prior MRI and has increased in size. The bladder wall is otherwise mildly trabeculated, consistent with post-radiation changes.

PROSTATE: Status post radiation changes. Fiducial markers are present.

OTHER: Status post-APR with end colostomy. No abdominopelvic lymphadenopathy. Degenerative changes in the spine.

IMPRESSION:
1.  A 1.2 x 1.1 cm enhancing nodule in the left posterior bladder wall, suspicious for urothelial carcinoma.
2.  No evidence of upper tract urothelial disease.
3.  No pelvic lymphadenopathy or distant metastatic disease.

RECOMMENDATION:
Cystoscopy with biopsy is recommended for definitive diagnosis.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Davis, MD
JSL Medical Center, Department of Radiology

Patient Id: p01

Date: 2019-06-07
Title: Operative Report - Cystoscopy and TURBT
---
PRE-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Bladder tumor

POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Bladder tumor

PROCEDURE:
1.  Cystoscopy
2.  Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor (TURBT)

SURGEON: Dr. Johnson, MD

ANESTHESIA: General

FINDINGS:
Flexible cystoscopy was performed. The urethra showed some mild stricturing but was traversable. The bladder mucosa showed diffuse post-radiation changes. A solitary, approximately 1.5 cm papillary tumor was identified on the posterior wall, to the left of the midline. The remainder of the bladder was clear.

PROCEDURE DESCRIPTION:
After induction of general anesthesia, the patient was placed in the dorsal lithotomy position. The resectoscope was introduced into the bladder. The papillary tumor identified on the posterior wall was resected in a fractionated manner. Papillary components were resected first, followed by a deep resection of the tumor base to include muscularis propria. Hemostasis was achieved with fulguration. The resected tissue was sent to pathology in separate containers ("papillary tumor" and "deep base"). At the end of the case, the bladder was irrigated clear. A Foley catheter was placed for continuous drainage.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and was transferred to the recovery room in stable condition.

SPECIMENS SENT:
1.  Bladder tumor, papillary component
2.  Bladder tumor, deep base

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Johnson, MD
JSL Medical Center, Department of Urology

Title: Genetics Consultation Note
---
PATIENT: Patient
ID: p01

REASON FOR CONSULTATION: Personal history of multiple primary cancers for evaluation of hereditary cancer syndrome.

BACKGROUND: This is a 64-year-old gentleman with a remarkable personal history of multiple malignancies, including:
- Rectal adenocarcinoma in 1987 (age 32)
- Appendiceal adenocarcinoma in 2005 (age 50)
- Prostate adenocarcinoma in 2015 (age 60)
- Newly diagnosed high-grade urothelial bladder cancer in 2019 (age 64)

FAMILY HISTORY: Significant for father with colon cancer and a sister with metastatic cancer of unknown primary.

ASSESSMENT: The patient's personal and family history are highly suggestive of Lynch Syndrome (Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer). His constellation of tumors (colorectal, appendiceal, urothelial, prostate) fits the spectrum of Lynch-associated malignancies. We discussed the implications of this diagnosis, including the need for lifelong surveillance and the potential risk for his family members.

PLAN:
1.  Proceed with germline genetic testing via a multi-gene panel (JSL-IMPACT) to identify a causative mutation. We specifically discussed looking for mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2).
2.  Patient provided informed consent for testing.
3.  Will schedule a follow-up visit to discuss the results and their implications for his future care and for his family.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Garcia, MD
JSL Medical Center, Cancer Genetics Service

===== Document 013 =====
Patient Id: p01
Doc Id: 013
Filename: p01/jsl_p01_013_pathology_doc.txt
Doc Type: pathology
Date: 2019-07-13
Title: JSL-IMPACT Secondary Germline Analysis Report
---
PATIENT: Patient
ID: p01
ACCESSION: [REDACTED]

TEST PERFORMED: Secondary Germline UPJHC-IMPACT (Analysis of 88 cancer predisposition genes)

SPECIMEN: DNA from Peripheral Blood

RESULTS: POSITIVE. A pathogenic variant was detected in the MSH2 gene.

VARIANT DETECTED:
Gene: MSH2 (NM_000251)
Variant: c.2038C>T (p.Arg680*)
Zygosity: Heterozygous
Classification: Pathogenic

INTERPRETATION:
This result confirms a diagnosis of Lynch Syndrome. The identified MSH2 nonsense variant (p.Arg680*) is a known pathogenic mutation that leads to a truncated, non-functional protein. Pathogenic variants in MSH2 are associated with a significantly increased lifetime risk for colorectal, endometrial, gastric, ovarian, urothelial, and other cancers.

This finding explains the patient's extensive personal history of multiple primary malignancies.

RECOMMENDATIONS:
-   Lifelong, enhanced surveillance for Lynch-associated cancers is critical.
-   Cascade testing for first-degree relatives is strongly recommended.
-   This information should guide all future oncologic management.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Roberts, PhD
JSL Lab, Molecular Diagnostics

Title: Operative Report - Re-staging TURBT
---
PRE-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: High-grade pT1 urothelial carcinoma of the bladder.

POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Same.

PROCEDURE: Re-staging Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor (TURBT).

SURGEON: Dr. Johnson, MD

INDICATION: Per standard of care, a re-staging TURBT is performed within 6 weeks of an initial pT1 diagnosis to ensure accurate staging and clear any residual disease before starting intravesical therapy.

FINDINGS AND PROCEDURE:
Cystoscopy revealed post-resection changes at the prior tumor site on the posterior wall. There was some erythematous and bullous-appearing tissue at the margins of the resection bed. The area was re-resected, taking care to obtain tissue from the margins and the deep base of the prior resection site. Hemostasis was achieved. A Foley catheter was placed.

SPECIMENS SENT:
1. Bladder, posterior wall re-resection

PLAN: Patient will be scheduled to begin a 6-week induction course of intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy following this procedure, pending pathology results.

Dr. Johnson, MD

Title: Urology Note - BCG Initiation
---
PATIENT: Patient
ID: p01

SUBJECTIVE:
Patient presents to initiate intravesical therapy for high-grade non-muscle invasive bladder cancer. He has recovered well from his re-staging TURBT on 07/20/2019. Pathology confirmed residual pTa high-grade disease. He has also been formally diagnosed with Lynch Syndrome (MSH2 mutation).

ASSESSMENT:
- High-Grade Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC), s/p TURBT x2. Ready for adjuvant therapy.
- Lynch Syndrome (MSH2 mutation).

PLAN:
1.  **BCG Therapy:** Begin 6-week induction course of intravesical BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin). Today marks Cycle 1 of 6.
2.  **Procedure:** The patient voided prior to the procedure. 50 mg of BCG in 50 mL saline was instilled into the bladder via a sterile catheter. The catheter was removed. The patient was instructed to retain the solution for 2 hours if possible, changing position every 15 minutes.
3.  **Side Effects:** Counseled on potential side effects, including urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria, hematuria, and low-grade fever. Advised on hygiene measures to prevent transmission.
4.  **Schedule:** He will return weekly for the next 5 weeks to complete the induction course.
5.  **Surveillance:** First surveillance cystoscopy will be scheduled 6 weeks after completion of the induction course.

Electronically Signed,
Dr. Johnson, MD
JSL Medical Center, Department of Urology
